questions.prompt: On an inpatient unit, what is the charge nurse's main role during a shift?

choices.a: Coordinating the unit's nursing assignments, bed flow and staffing for the shift
choices.b: Writing the physician team's admission orders
choices.c: Serving as the attending physician for the unit's patients
choices.d: Running the hospital's billing and insurance office

questions.explanation: The charge nurse coordinates the unit for the shift: nursing assignments, admissions and discharges, bed flow and escalation. Physicians write medical orders; the charge nurse is often the best first contact for unit logistics.
questions.learning_objective: Describe the charge nurse's coordinating role on an inpatient unit.

questions.prompt: You are about to follow your team into a patient's room. When should you clean your hands?

choices.a: Only if your hands look dirty
choices.b: On the way in and on the way out of the room, and before and after touching the patient or their surroundings
choices.c: Once at the start of the day, then gloves take over

questions.explanation: Clean your hands entering and leaving every room ("foam in, foam out"), and before and after contact with the patient or their surroundings. Gloves do not replace hand hygiene, and visibly soiled hands need soap and water rather than alcohol rub.
questions.learning_objective: Apply the hand-hygiene moments when entering and leaving a patient's room.

questions.prompt: During bedside rounds, where should a shadowing student usually stand?

choices.a: At the head of the bed, beside the patient's face
choices.b: Near the foot of the bed or the back of the room: able to observe without blocking the team or the patient
choices.c: In the doorway, holding the door open
choices.d: Sitting on the edge of the patient's bed

questions.explanation: A shadowing student observes from the foot of the bed or the back of the room. That keeps the path to the patient clear for the team, leaves the patient space, and still lets you see and hear. Never sit on a patient's bed.
questions.learning_objective: Choose an observer position that respects the patient and the team during rounds.

questions.prompt: A patient's door has a Contact Precautions sign. If your team asks you to come in, what should you do?

choices.a: Walk in quickly and avoid touching anything
choices.b: Clean your hands, put on a gown and gloves as the sign directs, and remove them before leaving the room
choices.d: Nothing extra; the precautions apply only to nurses

questions.explanation: Contact precautions mean a gown and gloves for anyone entering, with hand hygiene before putting them on and after taking them off at the doorway. Always read the door sign first; other precaution types need different equipment.
questions.learning_objective: Recognize contact-precaution signage and the protective equipment it requires.

questions.prompt: In a crowded elevator, a resident asks you what you thought of the patient you just saw. What is the best response?

choices.b: Suggest you talk it through somewhere private, such as the team workroom
choices.c: Share only the diagnosis and room number
choices.d: Share the case but leave out the patient's name

questions.explanation: Elevators, hallways and cafeterias are public spaces. Save patient discussion for a private area; details like a room number, age or diagnosis can identify someone even without a name.
questions.learning_objective: Protect patient privacy by keeping clinical discussion out of public spaces.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of reviewing a patient's chart in the EHR before rounds?

choices.a: To copy yesterday's note forward unchanged
choices.b: To catch up on what changed since the last visit: vital signs, new results, nursing notes and orders
choices.c: To change the patient's medication orders
choices.d: To print the chart to take home

questions.explanation: Chart review prepares the team to see the patient: overnight events, vital-sign trends, new labs and imaging, nursing notes and current orders. Notes are written fresh for each day, orders come from licensed prescribers, and charts never leave the hospital.
questions.learning_objective: Explain what chart review contributes to the daily workflow of an inpatient team.

questions.prompt: Which use of your student EHR access is appropriate?

choices.a: Looking up a classmate who was admitted last night
choices.b: Opening only the charts of patients you are involved with, as your role allows
choices.c: Photographing a lab table to study at home
choices.d: Letting a friend use your login to finish a task

questions.explanation: Access the records you need for the patients you are involved with, and nothing more. Every chart opened is logged and audited; photographs of patient information and shared logins are never appropriate.
questions.learning_objective: Describe appropriate, role-limited use of EHR access.
